title: Why Valtiendas tastes the way it does

lede.text: Most Valtiendas vineyards stand on a high plateau, at an average altitude above 800 m, where days and nights differ sharply in temperature. That swing raises the acidity, so the wines are fresher and livelier than those of nearby areas.

chapters.title: The high north of Segovia
paras: The zone lies in the north of Segovia province and covers 433.4 km². It takes in 16 municipalities, all in Segovia. Wine must be aged inside the same zone.

Vines here go back a long way. Traces of vineyards in northern Segovia date from the 12th century, and the strongest evidence is from the 15th century. In 1751 the Fuentidueña area had 710 hectares of vines, mostly for local drinking.

As neighbouring Ribera del Duero grew in the early 1990s, new vineyards were planted here with modern growing methods. New wineries were built too. In 2007 the zone was recognised as Vino de Calidad de Valtiendas, "quality wine of Valtiendas".

chapters.title: Long winters, big swings
paras: The climate is Mediterranean with continental influences. The average altitude is above 800 m, so winters are long and harsh and summers are mild.
Temperatures swing widely between day and night, mostly between August and September. Sun is strong at this height, and winds keep the grapes healthy.
Rain is not plentiful, at 400 to 500 mm a year. The soils hold water well, which makes up for it.

Ripening is slow and steady. The grapes build up plenty of anthocyanins and tannins, which show in the colour and structure of the wine. Aroma compounds build up too, which makes the wines more aromatic. The height has a cooling effect, and the wide temperature swing raises acidity.

chapters.title: Clay and pebbles on the páramo
paras: Most of the vineyard stands on the páramo, the high flat plateau. Soils across the zone generally have a medium texture and a lot of clay, above all on the páramo. The clay holds water and nutrients such as potassium.

A true carpet of rounded stones and pebbles covers the ground. It helps drainage and helps the bunches ripen. It also forms a natural mulch. The stones give the wines a mineral aroma that sets them apart.

chapters.title: Tempranillo first, in small yields
paras: Tempranillo, known locally as Tinta del País, leads. Reds and rosés both need at least 50% of it. Garnacha Tinta, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah are also allowed. Rosé may add the white Albillo Mayor.
Albillo is more productive than the reds, and growers look to it for higher acidity. It gives the rosés freshness.
Red yields are capped at 7,000 kg per hectare, and growers get about that from trellised vines. Albillo may reach 10,000 kg per hectare. Vines must be planted at 2,000 to 4,000 per hectare.

The wines are intense in colour and well structured, which favours ageing. Aged wines may carry Crianza, Reserva or Gran Reserva on the label, with ageing counted from 1 November of the harvest year. Rosés show fruit such as raspberry and blackberry, with floral notes.
